body:
From Delhi to the regional Sultanates

The Delhi Sultanate established an important early centre of monumental Indo-Islamic architecture. Its monuments demonstrate the growing use of true arches, domes, minars, inscriptions, fortified walls and large enclosed courtyards.

As political authority became distributed among regional Sultanates, builders adapted these features to different climates, available materials and established artistic traditions. This produced recognisable styles in Jaunpur, Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa and the Deccan.

The imperial style of Delhi

The Qutb complex is associated with the early Delhi Sultanate. It includes the Qutb Minar, Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque and the later Alai Darwaza. The Qutb Minar was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak in 1199; the Alai Darwaza was commissioned by Alauddin Khalji in 1311.

Under the Tughlaqs, several monumental structures emphasised massive walls and a comparatively restrained exterior. Sloping or battered walls are especially associated with Tughlaq fortification architecture.

Later, the Sayyid and Lodi periods produced important tomb architecture. The octagonal tomb, seen at monuments such as the tombs of Muhammad Shah Sayyid and Sikandar Lodi in Delhi, is a recognisable form. The use of square and octagonal plans illustrates variation within Sultanate tomb building.

Important regional styles and monuments

Region or schoolRecognisable featureImportant example
Jaunpur, Sharqi styleVery tall, imposing central entrance façadeAtala Masjid, Jaunpur
Bengal SultanateBrickwork, terracotta ornament and curved rooflinesRegional Bengal mosques
Malwa, ManduMassive forms, pavilions, local stone and adaptation to landscapeHindola Mahal, Jahaz Mahal, Hoshang Shah's tomb
Gujarat SultanateCarved pillars, brackets, lattice screens and regional motifsAhmedabad mosques and Sarkhej Roza
Deccani SultanatesMonumental domes, distinctive towers and regional ornamentGol Gumbaz, Bijapur; Charminar, Hyderabad

Jaunpur

The Atala Masjid at Jaunpur was completed in 1408 under Ibrahim Shah Sharqi. Its striking feature is the tall central entrance façade, which rises prominently before the domed prayer space. This characteristic façade distinguishes the Sharqi style from many Delhi and Gujarat examples.

Bengal

Medieval Bengal made extensive use of brick and terracotta because suitable building stone was less readily available in many areas. Mosque rooflines and cornices often adopted a curved form associated with regional thatched-roof traditions. The Mughals later adopted variations of the so-called Bangla roof in their own buildings.

Malwa and Mandu

Mandu, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, developed an important provincial style. The Hindola Mahal is known for its markedly sloping supporting walls, which create the impression of a swinging structure. The Jahaz Mahal, associated with Ghiyasuddin Khalji of Malwa, stands between water bodies and is popularly called the ship palace.

Hoshang Shah's tomb is another important Mandu monument, notable for its dome and ornamental stonework. Mandu's pavilions, palaces and water features show how buildings could be planned in relation to the surrounding terrain.

Deccani architecture

Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur, Karnataka, is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah of the Adil Shahi dynasty. Its enormous dome, corner towers and whispering gallery are major distinguishing features. It belongs to the Deccani Sultanate tradition, not the Mughal architectural group.

Charminar in Hyderabad was commissioned by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1591. Its name refers to its 4 prominent minarets. It is associated with the Qutb Shahi rulers of Golconda, not with a Mughal emperor.

Regional Sultanate architecture was not merely an imitation of Delhi. The Sharqi façade of Jaunpur, Bengal's curved roof forms, Mandu's landscape-sensitive buildings and Deccani monumental domes demonstrate distinct regional responses.

Prelims focus

  • Atala Masjid, Jaunpur: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi, completed in 1408.
  • Bengal Sultanate architecture commonly used brick, terracotta and curved cornices.
  • Hindola Mahal and Jahaz Mahal are associated with Mandu in Malwa.
  • Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur: tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah of the Adil Shahi dynasty.
  • Charminar, Hyderabad: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, 1591.
  • Trap: Gol Gumbaz and Charminar are associated with Deccani Sultanates, not Mughal emperors.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, pp. 110–118, 123; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, p. 72; Archaeological Survey of India, Qutb Minar and its Monuments, accessed 23 November 2026; District Administration, Jaunpur, Atala Masjid, monument description, accessed 23 November 2026; Delhi Tourism, Lodi Tomb, monument description, accessed 23 November 2026; Telangana Tourism, Charminar, monument description, accessed 23 November 2026.]

title: The Delhi Sultanate and Its Regional Architectural Schools

body:
How Gujarat developed a distinct Sultanate style

Gujarat provides one of the clearest examples of regional adaptation within Indo-Islamic architecture. Builders working for the Gujarat Sultans incorporated elements familiar from local Hindu and Jain building traditions into mosques, tombs and gateways.

Characteristic features include richly carved stone pillars, projecting brackets, lintels, pierced jali screens, ornamental panels, torana-like forms and motifs such as bells, chains, flowers and trees. These features appeared alongside Islamic requirements such as the qibla-oriented prayer hall and mihrab.

The combination did not make the buildings identical to temples. Their functions and overall arrangements remained appropriate to mosques or tombs, while many elements of their construction and decoration reflected the skills of local craftspeople.

Ahmedabad under Ahmad Shah

Sultan Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad in 1411 on the eastern bank of the Sabarmati River. The walled city developed around its fortifications, gates, markets, residential neighbourhoods, mosques and tombs. Its historic built environment preserves a major concentration of Gujarat Sultanate architecture.

The Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad was built in 1423–1424. It combines a large open courtyard with a richly supported prayer hall. The hall contains approximately 260 pillars supporting 15 domes, demonstrating how a forest of carved supports could be incorporated into a Sultanate mosque.

This use of many pillars and lintels is particularly significant: Indo-Islamic buildings were not restricted to entirely arcuate construction. Gujarat's masons continued to employ sophisticated trabeate techniques.

Sidi Saiyyed Mosque and its famous jali

The Sidi Saiyyed Mosque in Ahmedabad was completed in 1573, during the political transition from Gujarat Sultanate rule to Mughal control. It is celebrated for its finely carved stone screens, especially the intertwined branches of the tree-of-life jali.

This monument is an excellent example for distinguishing jali from other ornament: the design is physically perforated through the stone, rather than painted or created only with coloured-stone inlay.

Sarkhej Roza

Sarkhej Roza, near Ahmedabad, is an important ensemble of tombs, a mosque and associated structures. It is closely connected with the Sufi saint Shaikh Ahmad Khattu, whose tomb is a major 15th-century monument of Gujarat.

The complex illustrates the regional preference for finely worked stone, jalis, carved brackets and careful relationships between buildings and open spaces. Its tomb architecture is an important example of provincial Indo-Islamic design.

Champaner-Pavagadh

Champaner, near Pavagadh in present-day Gujarat, became an important Sultanate centre under Mahmud Begada, who conquered the hill-fortress in 1484 and developed the area as a capital.

The Jami Masjid of Champaner is a distinguished example of the Gujarat Sultanate tradition. Its monumental entrance, carved pillars, ornamented prayer spaces and combinations of regional craftsmanship with Islamic architectural planning make it especially useful for identifying the style.

The wider Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park contains fortifications, religious buildings, water structures and other remains from several periods. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2004. The designation applies to the archaeological park as a whole, not only to the Jami Masjid.

Historic Ahmedabad and World Heritage recognition

The Historic City of Ahmadabad was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2017. The recognition concerns the historic urban ensemble, including the Sultanate-period monuments and the distinctive residential fabric of the old city.

As of 23 November 2026, both the Historic City of Ahmadabad and Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park are inscribed World Heritage properties. Their inscription years are different and refer to different heritage areas.

Prelims focus

  • Ahmedabad was founded by Sultan Ahmad Shah in 1411.
  • Ahmedabad Jama Masjid: built in 1423–1424; approximately 260 pillars and 15 domes.
  • Sidi Saiyyed Mosque: completed in 1573; famous for the tree-of-life jali.
  • Sarkhej Roza is associated with the Sufi saint Shaikh Ahmad Khattu.
  • Champaner developed under Mahmud Begada after the conquest of 1484.
  • Trap: Champaner-Pavagadh was inscribed in 2004; the Historic City of Ahmadabad was inscribed in 2017.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, pp. 110–111; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic City of Ahmadabad, Outstanding Universal Value and inscription details, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, Outstanding Universal Value and inscription details, accessed 23 November 2026; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Jama Masjid and Sidi Saiyyed Mosque, monument descriptions, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A Gujarat Sultanate mosque could combine a courtyard and prayer hall with locally familiar carved pillars and screens.

title: Gujarat Sultanate Architecture: Ahmedabad, Sarkhej and Champaner

body:
The development of Mughal architectural identity

The Mughal rulers inherited architectural ideas from Central Asian, Persian, Delhi Sultanate and regional Indian traditions. Their monuments combined these influences in different proportions. Two important developments were the use of monumental tombs within formal gardens and the adaptation of Indian pillared and bracketed structures in imperial palaces.

Humayun's Tomb in Delhi and the architectural projects of Akbar provide important foundations for understanding the mature Mughal style.

Humayun's Tomb, Delhi

Humayun's Tomb was constructed during the 1560s–1570s in memory of the Mughal emperor Humayun. It is a pioneering example of the large Mughal dynastic garden tomb.

The monument combines red sandstone with white marble. Its high central dome and monumental arched entrance, known as a pishtaq, create a strong central emphasis. The tomb stands within a formally organised chahar bagh, or four-part garden.

The building is associated with the hasht bihisht, or eight-paradises, arrangement. In this design, a principal central space is surrounded by 8 subsidiary chambers or spaces. This internal organisation is different from the fourfold division of the surrounding garden.

The tomb's central position within the formal garden is a particularly important distinction from the later arrangement of the Taj Mahal, where the mausoleum stands at the river-facing end of the garden.

Agra Fort under Akbar

Akbar undertook major construction at Agra Fort from 1565. The fort became an important imperial residence and administrative centre. Its substantial red sandstone construction is characteristic of Akbar's architectural patronage.

Agra Fort was not built in one phase by one emperor. Later Mughal rulers, particularly Shah Jahan, introduced or altered buildings within the complex, including structures with extensive marble work.

Thus, a monument within Agra Fort may belong to a later phase even though Akbar was responsible for the major development of the fort.

Fatehpur Sikri: Akbar's planned imperial centre

Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra, was developed as an imperial centre by Akbar in the late 16th century, particularly during the 1570s and early 1580s. The complex includes palaces, audience halls, a congregational mosque, gateways and religious buildings.

Important monuments include the Buland Darwaza, Jama Masjid, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas and the tomb of Shaikh Salim Chishti.

The complex is notable for its red sandstone buildings and widespread use of pillars, lintels, carved brackets, projecting eaves and chhatris. These features demonstrate the continuing importance of trabeate construction within Mughal architecture.

Architectural elements at Fatehpur Sikri also reflect traditions associated with Gujarat and Malwa. For example, carved columns and supporting brackets reveal the influence of regional Indian craftsmanship.

Buland Darwaza and Gujarat

The Buland Darwaza is a monumental gateway at Fatehpur Sikri. It is commonly associated with Akbar's military success in Gujarat. Accounts differ on the precise dating of its completion, so its historical association is more secure as a basic examination fact than a single unqualified construction year.

Humayun's Tomb: an imperial tomb in a formal garden. Agra Fort: a major Akbar-era fortified palace and administrative complex. Fatehpur Sikri: Akbar's planned imperial centre with strong regional Indian architectural influences.

Prelims focus

  • Humayun's Tomb is in Delhi and combines red sandstone with white marble.
  • Hasht bihisht refers to a central space with 8 surrounding spaces.
  • Humayun's Tomb stands centrally within a formal chahar bagh garden.
  • Akbar began major construction at Agra Fort in 1565.
  • Fatehpur Sikri was developed by Akbar in the late 16th century.
  • Trap: Buland Darwaza is at Fatehpur Sikri, not at Agra Fort.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, pp. 66–72; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, pp. 109–111; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Humayun's Tomb, Delhi, monument description, accessed 23 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, monument descriptions, accessed 23 November 2026.]
